subject: Service credit for the November 12 outage — confirm within 48 hours
preview: Following the recent service disruption, we are issuing account credits to affected users. Confirm your details to receive yours...
body_html:
Dear Customer,

Following the service disruption on November 12 that affected mail, chat and file access, we are issuing a goodwill service credit to all affected accounts.

To receive your credit, please confirm your account and billing details within 48 hours. Unconfirmed accounts will not be credited.

red_flags.title: The outage used as the hook
red_flags.explanation: Attackers rush out 'compensation' emails right after a well-known outage, while everyone is expecting contact and feeling owed something. The timing is the trap.

red_flags.title: Asks for billing details via a link
red_flags.explanation: A real provider already has your billing on file and credits it automatically. Being sent to a page to 'confirm' card details is harvesting, not a refund.

red_flags.title: Reply-to doesn't match the sender
red_flags.explanation: The reply address sits on a different lookalike domain from the 'from' line.

what_to_do: Don't claim outage 'credits' through an email link. Any genuine credit appears on your next bill automatically.
Check the provider's official status page, which you reach yourself, for what really happened.
Report it; a wave of these always follows a big outage.
lesson: After every major outage comes a wave of 'service credit' and 'compensation' lures. Real credits are automatic; a link asking for billing details is a scam.

subject: Re-verify your account to restore access after the outage
preview: As part of recovery from the November 12 outage, affected accounts must be re-verified before access is fully restored...
body_html:
Dear User,

As part of our recovery from the November 12 service outage, affected accounts must be re-verified before access is fully restored. For your security, sign in to confirm your identity.

Accounts not re-verified within 24 hours will remain suspended.

red_flags.title: Outage used to justify a sign-in
red_flags.explanation: An outage never requires you to re-verify or re-enter your password. Recovery happens on the provider's side, not by making users log in through a link.

red_flags.title: Lookalike sign-in domain
red_flags.explanation: The sign-in link goes to an outside lookalike domain built to capture your password, not your real provider.

red_flags.title: 24-hour suspension threat
red_flags.explanation: The lockout deadline is pressure to make you sign in before you think.

what_to_do: Never re-verify or sign in from an outage email. Open the app the way you normally do.
If access really is affected, it comes back on its own as the provider restores service.
Check the official status page yourself, and report this message.
lesson: "Re-verify your account after the outage" is credential phishing. Outages are fixed by the provider; they never need you to log in through a link.

subject: Action: run the Outage Recovery Assistant to resync your mailbox
preview: Mail delayed by the November 12 outage can be resynced using the recovery assistant attached. Download and run it to restore missing messages...
body_html:
Dear Employee,

Some mail was delayed during the November 12 outage. To restore any missing messages, download and run the Outage Recovery Assistant attached, then let it resync your mailbox.

Please run it today so your inbox is fully caught up.

red_flags.title: An executable 'recovery tool'
red_flags.explanation: A .exe attached to an outage email is malware. No real recovery needs you to download and run a program a mailbox resyncs itself on the server.

red_flags.title: Outage used to justify running it
red_flags.explanation: The outage story is there to make a dangerous download feel urgent and reasonable.

red_flags.title: Lookalike support domain
red_flags.explanation: The real service desk doesn't send from brightlinecorp-support.example.

what_to_do: Never download or run 'recovery', 'patch' or 'resync' tools sent by email, especially .exe, .iso or script files.
Mail delayed by an outage catches up on its own once service is restored.
If you ran it, disconnect and contact IT immediately; report the message either way.
lesson: Outage 'recovery tools' are malware in a helpful disguise. Delayed mail resyncs itself; you never need to run a program to fix an outage.

subject: Your mailbox is still in the outage backlog — request priority restore
preview: Some mailboxes remain in the restoration backlog after the November 12 outage. Verify ownership to move yours to the priority queue...
body_html:
Hello,

Some mailboxes remain in the restoration backlog following the November 12 outage. To move your mailbox to the priority queue and restore it sooner, please verify ownership below.

red_flags.title: A fake 'priority queue'
red_flags.explanation: You cannot pay or 'verify' your way to the front of a real restoration queue. The offer exists only to make you click.

red_flags.title: Verify-ownership link
red_flags.explanation: 'Verify ownership' leads to a sign-in page that captures your credentials.

red_flags.title: Outside status domain
red_flags.explanation: cloud-status-updates.example is not your provider's real status page.

what_to_do: Ignore 'priority restore' offers; restoration order is not something you can change by clicking a link.
Watch the official status page you already know for genuine progress.
Don't verify anything, and report the message.
lesson: "Jump the restoration queue" is bait unique to outages. No provider lets you skip ahead by verifying through a link; it only harvests your login.

subject: URGENT: Confidential Vendor Settlement Required Today
preview: I am currently locked in urgent board negotiations and cannot take calls. We need to settle an emergency invoice...
body_html:
Team,

I am currently locked in urgent board negotiations and cannot take calls. We need to settle an emergency invoice with our primary hardware vendor immediately to avoid supply chain termination.

Please wire $48,500 to the escrow account details provided in the secure portal link below within the next 2 hours. Do not discuss this with local finance yet to maintain confidentiality.

red_flags.title: External Lookalike Domain
red_flags.explanation: Uses a typo-squatted domain (corp-secure-auth.example) rather than the corporate domain.

red_flags.title: Urgency & Secrecy
red_flags.explanation: Pressures the target to bypass standard multi-person financial controls and keep the request secret from colleagues.

red_flags.title: Generic Call to Action
red_flags.explanation: Generic anchor text pointing to an external credential-harvesting or credential-stuffing landing page.

what_to_do: Stop. A genuine executive will not ask you to bypass finance controls or keep a payment secret.
Verify the request out of band: call the executive or finance on a number you already have, not one in the email.
Report the message to your security team and do not click the link or move any money.
lesson: Urgency plus secrecy plus a payment request is the signature of business email compromise. Slow down and verify through a channel you already trust.

subject: Action Required: Mandatory Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) Re-Registration
preview: As part of our enterprise security hardening schedule following recent threat intelligence bulletins, all employees must re-verify...
body_html:
Dear Employee,

As part of our enterprise security hardening schedule following recent threat intelligence bulletins, all employees must re-verify their authentication tokens within 24 hours. Failure to update will result in account suspension and loss of email access.

Click below to sync your hardware token or authenticator app:

red_flags.title: Suspicious Sender Infrastructure
red_flags.explanation: Hosted on an unrelated external domain (defender-auth-alerts.example).

red_flags.title: Coercive Deadlines
red_flags.explanation: Threatens account lockout to trigger panic and quick compliance.

red_flags.title: Credential Harvesting Link
red_flags.explanation: Directs users away from the legitimate internal IDP login portal to an external harvesting clone.

what_to_do: Never re-register MFA from a link in an email. Open your authenticator or sign-in portal the way you normally do.
Check the real sender domain; security notices come from your own IT, not an outside address.
Report it and let the deadline pass. Genuine IT will not lock you out for ignoring a suspicious email.
lesson: A countdown to account lockout is pressure, not policy. Go to the known internal portal yourself.

subject: Critical Notice: Enterprise Software Subscription Expiring Today
preview: Your department's annual enterprise software license agreement has expired due to a billing failure...
body_html:
Hello Administrator,

Your department's annual enterprise software license agreement has expired due to a billing failure. To prevent disruption to your design and documentation workflows, please review and execute the attached updated licensing agreement script.

red_flags.title: Malicious File Attachment
red_flags.explanation: Uses an ISO or archived executable container designed to bypass email gateway macro inspection and drop remote-access trojans or infostealer payloads.

red_flags.title: Urgently Framed Business Disruption
red_flags.explanation: Leverages common enterprise software names to induce quick downloading without security scrutiny.

what_to_do: Do not open .iso or other executable or archive attachments you were not expecting.
Licensing is handled by your IT or procurement team, not by a billing email with an attached 'script'.
Report the message so the attachment can be analysed safely.
lesson: An ISO or archived executable in an unexpected 'invoice' or 'license' email is a classic malware dropper.

subject: Updated Remote Work Expense Guidelines for Q4
preview: Please review the updated Q4 remote work and office equipment expense policy attached to this email.
body_html:
Hi Everyone,

Please review the updated Q4 remote work and office equipment expense policy attached to this email. The internal finance wiki has also been updated with the new submission codes. If you have any questions, reach out via our internal Slack channel #hr-support.
safe_reasons: Internal Domain Alignment: Sent entirely from the verified internal corporate domain (brightlinecorp.example).
Standard Document Format: Uses a safe, non-executable document format (.pdf) rather than scripts or ISOs.
Alternative Contact Channels: Directs inquiries to an official internal communication channel rather than demanding immediate external action.
what_to_do: Trusting genuine messages is part of the job. This one is safe to read and act on.
If anything ever looks off, confirm through a channel you already know, like the #hr-support Slack channel named here, rather than a link in the message.
Open attachments like a .pdf as normal; be wary only of executable or archive formats such as .iso, .exe or script files.
lesson: A message from your real internal domain that points you to official channels and asks for none of your secrets is usually exactly what it says it is.

subject: Scheduled Maintenance: VPN Gateway Upgrades This Sunday
preview: Our Network Operations Center will perform scheduled maintenance on our primary VPN gateways this Sunday from 02:00 to 04:00 EST.
body_html:
Team,

Our Network Operations Center will perform scheduled maintenance on our primary VPN gateways this Sunday from 02:00 to 04:00 EST. Brief service interruptions may occur. No user action or password reset is required.

Check our status page at status.brightlinecorp.example for live updates.
safe_reasons: No Credential Requests: Explicitly states that no user action, credential entry, or password reset is required.
Informational Tone: Standard operational notification providing advance notice through internal infrastructure channels.
what_to_do: Nothing. A maintenance notice that asks for no action and no password is informational, so just note the window.
Remember that genuine IT notices tell you when NOT to act; scams almost always demand that you do something urgently.
If you want to confirm, visit the known internal status page yourself rather than following a link someone sends you.
lesson: Real operational notices inform you; they do not pressure you to enter credentials or reset a password out of the blue.

subject: Daily Automated Threat Intelligence & Ransomware Briefing
preview: Today's cross-sector briefing covering edge device zero-days and container OpenSSH audits has been generated.
body_html:
Automated Security Operations Briefing:

Today's cross-sector briefing covering edge device zero-days (such as Veltra CVE-2026-107441) and container OpenSSH audits has been successfully generated and synchronized to your secure Brightline Drive folder and master CSV log.
safe_reasons: Contextual Consistency: Aligned with internal engineering workflows, utilizing trusted internal automation pipelines and verified cloud storage endpoints.
what_to_do: Nothing unusual is needed. This is your own automation posting its daily briefing to a known internal location.
If you want the report, open the shared drive the way you normally do rather than only trusting the link.
Stay aware that attackers imitate this style, so still check the sender and destination before acting on any 'briefing'.
lesson: Expected, context-appropriate automation from your own internal systems is the normal background hum of a secure workplace.

subject: Updated remittance details for invoice INV-20451
preview: Please note our banking details have recently changed. Kindly update your records before settling the attached invoice...
body_html:
Dear Accounts Payable,

Please note our banking details have recently changed. Kindly update your records and remit payment for the attached invoice (INV-20451, $21,480.00) to our new account below before the due date to avoid a late fee.

New account: Sort 40-21-09 · Acct 7781254490 · Ref INV-20451

Apologies for any inconvenience. Kindly confirm once your records are updated.

red_flags.title: Change of bank details
red_flags.explanation: A supplier emailing new payment details out of the blue is the most common form of invoice fraud. The attacker has spoofed or taken over the vendor's email.

red_flags.title: Reply-to does not match the sender
red_flags.explanation: Replies would go to a different, lookalike billing domain, not the address the mail claims to be from.

red_flags.title: Pressure to pay quickly
red_flags.explanation: The 'before the due date to avoid a late fee' line is there to rush the change through before anyone checks.

what_to_do: Never change a supplier's bank details on an email instruction alone.
Call the vendor on a number you already have on file (not one from this email) to confirm any change.
Require a second approver for payment-detail changes, and report this message.
lesson: A new bank account in an email is the signature of invoice fraud. Verify every payment-detail change out of band, on a trusted number.

subject: Action needed: re-validate your authenticator within 24 hours
preview: Scan the code below with your phone to re-validate your multi-factor authentication. Unvalidated accounts will be suspended...
body_html:
Dear Employee,

Our records show your multi-factor authentication needs to be re-validated. Scan the QR code below with your phone's camera and follow the steps. Accounts not validated within 24 hours will be suspended.

Thank you for helping keep our systems secure.

red_flags.title: A QR code hides the real link
red_flags.explanation: You cannot read where a QR code goes before you scan it, and it moves you onto your phone, away from your computer's protections. That is exactly why attackers use them.

red_flags.title: Lookalike sender domain
red_flags.explanation: Real IT security mail comes from your own domain, not brightlinecorp-it.example.

red_flags.title: Lockout deadline
red_flags.explanation: 'Suspended within 24 hours' is pressure to make you scan before you think.

what_to_do: Don't scan QR codes in emails. Re-validate MFA from inside your authenticator app the way you normally do.
If you're unsure, check with IT through a channel you already trust.
Remember a QR code is just a link you can't see, so treat it with the same caution as any link.
lesson: Quishing puts a link you can't preview onto a phone outside corporate protection. Don't scan codes from email; act inside the real app.

subject: Change to my direct deposit account
preview: Hi, I've recently switched banks. Please update my direct deposit to the new account below effective this pay cycle...
body_html:
Hi Payroll,

I've recently switched banks. Please update my direct deposit to the new account below, effective this pay cycle, so my salary isn't delayed.

New account: Routing 021000021 · Account 554120983

Please confirm once it's done. Thanks,
Marcus Bell

red_flags.title: Request comes from outside the company
red_flags.explanation: A genuine employee's request would come from their corporate account, not an outside secure-mailbox.example address.

red_flags.title: Direct-deposit change by email
red_flags.explanation: Changing where someone's salary is paid, with no identity check, is exactly what payroll-diversion fraud wants.

red_flags.title: Pressure to beat this pay cycle
red_flags.explanation: The deadline exists so the money is redirected before the real employee notices.

what_to_do: Verify any direct-deposit change with the employee in person or on a number from your own HR records.
Never action a banking change from an email alone, especially from an outside address.
Report it; the real employee's identity may be being impersonated.
lesson: Payroll diversion redirects a real person's salary with a single emailed 'bank change'. Always verify the employee through a known channel first.

subject: New voicemail from (800) 555-0188 — duration 00:42
preview: You have received a new voice message. Sign in to the secure portal to listen before it is deleted...
body_html:
You have received a new voice message.

Caller: (800) 555-0188 · Duration: 00:42 · Received today.

Sign in to the secure portal to listen. Unheard messages are deleted after 48 hours. You may be asked to complete a quick security check to continue.

red_flags.title: Unexpected voicemail by email
red_flags.explanation: A link to 'listen' to a voicemail, from an outside service you don't use, leads to a fake sign-in page, not a message.

red_flags.title: The 'security check' is a cloak
red_flags.explanation: The promised CAPTCHA or 'security check' is there to make the page feel legitimate and to hide it from automated scanners.

red_flags.title: Outside sender and deletion deadline
red_flags.explanation: An unfamiliar external domain plus a '48 hours or deleted' deadline is pressure to click fast.

what_to_do: Listen to voicemail through your actual phone or your company's real voicemail system, never a link in an email.
A CAPTCHA or 'security check' before a login is a trick to make a fake page look real; it is not reassurance.
Don't click, and report the message.
lesson: A 'you have a voicemail' email with a sign-in link is credential phishing. The CAPTCHA step is camouflage, not safety.

subject: You have a document to review and sign: Q4 Vendor Agreement
preview: A document is waiting for your signature. Review and sign before the request expires in 48 hours...
body_html:
Hello,

A document, Q4 Vendor Agreement, is waiting for your electronic signature. Please review and sign before this request expires in 48 hours.

If you believe you received this in error, no action is needed.

red_flags.title: A document you weren't expecting
red_flags.explanation: E-signature lures count on you clicking quickly so a contract isn't held up. If you weren't expecting it, be suspicious.

red_flags.title: Link leads to a sign-in, not a document
red_flags.explanation: The button goes to an external sign-in page built to capture your password, not to a real signing service.

red_flags.title: Expiry countdown
red_flags.explanation: 'Expires in 48 hours' is manufactured urgency.

what_to_do: Only open signing requests you're expecting, and go to the signing service directly rather than via the email link.
Check who the sender really is; a genuine request names a person and context you recognise.
If in doubt, confirm with the supposed sender on a known channel.
lesson: Fake e-signature requests exploit the habit of signing fast. Open them only when expected, and reach the service directly.

subject: A file has been shared with you: 2026 Bonus Structure.xlsx
preview: Someone shared a document with you. Open it to view the file...
body_html:
A file has been shared with you.

2026 Bonus Structure.xlsx · shared just now

You are receiving this because a document was shared with your address.

red_flags.title: A too-tempting filename
red_flags.explanation: 'Bonus Structure' is bait: curiosity about pay makes people click before they think.

red_flags.title: Not your real drive
red_flags.explanation: The share comes from an outside lookalike domain, not the file service your company actually uses.

red_flags.title: No named sharer
red_flags.explanation: A genuine share names the person who shared it; 'someone shared a file' is a red flag, and the button leads to a fake sign-in.

what_to_do: Open shared files from inside your real file-storage app, not from an email link.
Check who shared it; if no real person is named, treat it as phishing.
Be extra wary of lures about pay, bonuses or layoffs; curiosity is the hook.
lesson: Shared-file lures use curiosity and a lookalike drive. Open documents from your real storage app, not an email button.

subject: Quick favour — are you available?
preview: Are you at your desk? I need you to handle something discreetly for me. I'm in meetings and can't take calls...
body_html:
Hi,

Are you at your desk? I need you to handle something discreetly. Please pick up five $100 gift cards for a client appreciation gesture and send me the codes by reply. I'm stuck in back-to-back meetings and can't take calls. I'll approve the reimbursement afterwards.

Thanks,
Dana

red_flags.title: Lookalike executive address
red_flags.explanation: The 'from' and the reply-to sit on outside lookalike domains, not your real corporate domain.

red_flags.title: Gift cards requested by email
red_flags.explanation: No genuine executive asks staff to buy gift cards and send the codes. This is a classic, and the codes are untraceable cash.

red_flags.title: Secrecy plus 'can't call'
red_flags.explanation: 'Discreetly' and 'can't take calls' exist to stop you verifying with anyone.

what_to_do: Treat any gift-card request as a scam, however senior the sender appears.
Verify through a channel you already trust before acting; a real executive won't mind.
Report it, so others who got the same message are warned.
lesson: The gift-card ask is one of the most reliable scam tells there is. Verify out of band and report; never buy or send codes.

subject: RESEND: Password expiry — please use the corrected link
preview: Our earlier message contained a broken link. Please use the corrected link below to reset your password before it expires today...
body_html:
Dear Employee,

Apologies — our earlier password-expiry email contained a broken link. Please use the corrected link below to reset your password before it expires today.

red_flags.title: The 'resend a corrected link' trick
red_flags.explanation: Clone phishing copies a routine email you half-expect and 'resends' it with the attacker's link. The familiarity is the trap.

red_flags.title: Lookalike support domain
red_flags.explanation: The real service desk doesn't send from brightlinecorp-support.example.

red_flags.title: Reset link in an email
red_flags.explanation: Password resets should start from you, at the known portal, not from a link someone sends.

what_to_do: Reset passwords only by going to your known sign-in portal yourself.
Be suspicious of 'resend' or 'corrected link' framing; it's used to make a cloned email feel real.
Check the sender domain and report anything that doesn't match.
lesson: Clone phishing mimics a message you were expecting and swaps in a bad link. Start sensitive actions yourself, from the known portal.

subject: Keep your session active: enter your verification code
preview: To avoid being signed out, open the sign-in page and enter the verification code below...
body_html:
Dear Employee,

To avoid being signed out during our scheduled maintenance, please open the sign-in page and enter the verification code below to keep your session active.

Your verification code: BXQ-7421

This prevents an interruption to your access.

red_flags.title: You're told to enter a code you didn't ask for
red_flags.explanation: Codes are meant to come to you after you start a sign-in. A code sent to you to type into a login screen means you'd be approving the attacker's device.

red_flags.title: Lookalike sender
red_flags.explanation: The sender sits on an outside lookalike domain, not your real IT.

red_flags.title: 'Keep your session active' pressure
red_flags.explanation: The maintenance/lockout story is there to get you to enter the code quickly.

what_to_do: Never enter a code that someone emailed you into a sign-in page.
Only type a code that you requested yourself, into a login you started.
Report it; device-code phishing authorises the attacker's device to act as you.
lesson: If an email hands you a code to type into a login, it's device-code phishing. Only ever use codes you asked for, in a sign-in you began.

subject: Notice: you are eligible for a tax refund of $842.60
preview: Our records show you are owed a refund. Confirm your details through our secure portal within 5 business days...
body_html:
Dear Taxpayer,

Our records show you are eligible for a refund of $842.60. To receive it, confirm your identity and bank details through our secure portal within 5 business days, or the refund will be forfeited.

red_flags.title: Tax agencies don't email refunds like this
red_flags.explanation: Real tax bodies contact you by official post and don't ask you to 'claim' a refund through an emailed link.

red_flags.title: Unofficial domain
red_flags.explanation: nrs-gov-portal.example is not an official government domain; it's built to harvest your identity and bank details.

red_flags.title: 'Forfeit in 5 days' pressure
red_flags.explanation: A countdown with a threat of losing money is designed to override your caution.

what_to_do: Never claim a refund through a link in an email.
Go to the tax authority's official website yourself, or call them on a number you look up independently.
Delete and report; a real refund never depends on you acting within days.
lesson: Refund and 'overdue tax' emails impersonate authorities to harvest identity and bank details. Use the official site directly, never the email's link.

subject: Open enrollment for 2027 benefits starts Monday
preview: Open enrollment runs 16-30 November. Review your options on the intranet benefits portal. No action needed if you're keeping your current plan...
body_html:
Hi everyone,

Open enrollment for 2027 benefits runs from 16-30 November. You can review your options and make any changes on the benefits portal, which is linked from the People page on the intranet.

No action is needed if you're keeping your current plan. Questions? Ask in the #people-help channel and someone will help.
safe_reasons: Internal Domain Alignment: Sent from the verified internal corporate domain (brightlinecorp.example).
No Credential Pressure: Points you to the intranet you already use rather than a link to sign in, and asks for nothing secret.
Alternative Contact Channel: Directs questions to a known internal channel, with a clear deadline but no threat.
what_to_do: This is safe to act on. Reach the benefits portal through the intranet the way you normally do.
If you're keeping your current plan, you don't need to do anything.
Genuine HR notices give you a deadline and a helpful channel, never a threat or a login link.
lesson: A notice from your real internal domain that points you to the intranet and asks for nothing secret is what genuine internal mail looks like.
